title: Maslow Was Right: What His Theory Can Teach Us about Moving Ahead
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing in the first weeks of pandemic school closures, Stuart argues that teachers should pause the stream of curricular objectives and attend first to students' basic needs, using Maslow's hierarchy as a guide. He reads Maslow as describing partial, overlapping satisfaction of needs rather than a rigid pyramid, picturing the lower levels as sieves that let motivation drip down to higher ones. He applies this to physiological needs (communicating food access and encouraging walks), safety (limiting news consumption, with a confession about his own news habit), and love (genuine connection through notes to students and colleagues). The piece frames stabilizing these three levels as the first job before academic demands resume.
points: Maslow's own 1943 framing is partial satisfaction across all needs, which makes the hierarchy a gradient, not a pyramid of steps.
In a crisis the physiological, safety, and love needs of students and staff are destabilized, so stabilizing them comes before curriculum.
Concrete moves include exhaustive communication about food access, walking, a five-minute daily news limit, and daily notes of appreciation.
The author models vulnerability by admitting his own relapse into news addiction.
quotes: It’s possible that right now isn’t the best time to obsess about providing a continuous stream of curricular objectives for our students. That time will come, but it’s probably not now.

Rather, Maslow argued that “normal” people “are partially satisfied in all their basic needs and partially unsatisfied in all their basic needs at the same time.” The most useful way to think of Maslow’s hierarchy, then, is in terms of “decreasing percentages of satisfaction as we go up the hierarchy.
Here’s the thing: for all of us, the physiological and safety and love sieves have gone haywire this week. Our cognitive, emotional, and spiritual inboxes are flooded with NOISE.

So in the midst of the present mayhem as schools and states around the world debate about equity and access and distance learning, I think we owe some thought to Maslow. The stabilization of these top three sieves is Job One.

Safety: Once we all understand how the virus spreads and what social distancing means, let’s turn off the news. Five minutes per day is plenty. The news isn’t designed to make us informed citizens. Remember — it’s designed to sell our eyeballs to advertisers.

Love: Moments of genuine connection always matter, but they’re uniquely important now. So, with our students and colleagues and family members, the goal is having conversations or sending notes that communicate that we value, know, and respect them.
